title: Mapping the spatial variability of subsurface resistivity by using vertical electrical sounding data and geostatistical analysis at Borena Area, Ethiopia
author: Abdulkadir, Fisseha
materials: provide CPs and derived parameters at VES (V-

steps.title: Collect VES data in field
steps.instruction: Conduct vertical electrical sounding (VES) surveys in three phases over the Borena area using a Schlumberger array; use a maximum half‑current electrode separation (AB/2) of 1000 m to reach potential water‑bearing horizons; space survey lines and sounding points to evenly cover the plains and any structural features; acquire approximately 288 VES soundings.

steps.title: Smooth apparent resistivity curves
steps.instruction: Apply the smoothing routine (implemented in the provided Python code) to each apparent‑resistivity‑versus‑AB/2 curve to minimise noise before further analysis.

steps.title: Determine characteristic points
steps.instruction: Compute first and second derivatives of each smoothed VES curve; locate inflection points (where the second derivative equals zero) and extreme points (local maxima or minima where the second derivative changes sign); also record the curve end points; label them CP‑1, CP‑2 … CP‑N as illustrated in Fig. 2.

steps.title: Assign depths and resistivities to CPs
steps.instruction: For each CP, calculate its depth as one‑quarter of the electrode spacing that produced the point (depth = AB/4). Assign apparent resistivity to a CP using the resistivity of the preceding CP, except for the first and last points which retain their own values. Example for VES V‑112 (Table 2): CP‑1 depth 0.75 m, ρ = 8.57 Ω·m; CP‑2 depth 3.26 m, ρ = 8.75 Ω·m; CP‑3 depth 5.76 m, ρ = 4.26 Ω·m; CP‑4 depth 12.02 m, ρ = 4.53 Ω·m; CP‑5 depth 29.56 m, ρ = 5.33 Ω·m; CP‑6 depth 250 m, ρ = 47.09 Ω·m.

steps.title: Log‑transform resistivity values
steps.instruction: Apply a logarithmic transformation to all CP apparent‑resistivity values to stabilise variance and eliminate negative values before variogram modelling.

steps.title: Compute experimental variograms
steps.instruction: For each depth interval (0‑5, 5‑10, 10‑20, 20‑40, 40‑60, 60‑80, 80‑110, 110‑140, 140‑170, 170‑210, 210‑240, 240‑270, 280‑310, 310‑350, 500 m), calculate the experimental semivariogram γ(h)=½ N(h)⁻¹ ∑[Z(xᵢ)−Z(xᵢ+h)]² using lag distances appropriate to the sampling spacing of 1‑5 km.

steps.title: Fit standard variogram models
steps.instruction: Fit spherical, Gaussian, exponential and power models to each experimental variogram using iterative re‑weighted least squares; compute RMSE for each fit and select the model with the smallest RMSE. Record the nugget, sill, range, nugget‑to‑sill ratio and spatial‑correlation class as in Table 3 (e.g., 0‑5 m: spherical, nugget 1.2, sill 1.98, range 700 m, nugget/sill 0.61, moderate; 5‑10 m: spherical, nugget 1.5, sill 2.65, range 454 m, nugget/sill 0.57, moderate; …; 500 m: spherical, nugget 0.22, sill 0.57, range 700 m, nugget/sill 0.39, high).

steps.title: Perform ordinary kriging
steps.instruction: Using the selected variogram parameters for each depth interval, execute ordinary kriging interpolation (e.g., via SAGA GIS) to estimate resistivity at unsampled locations across the study area, employing the spatial coordinates of the CPs as input data.

steps.title: Create iso‑apparent resistivity maps
steps.instruction: Generate two‑dimensional iso‑apparent resistivity maps for the pseudo‑depths AB/2 = 13.5, 45, 66, 100, 150, 220, 330, 500, 750 and 1000 m by plotting the kriged resistivity values; produce stacked depth‑section maps to visualise lateral and vertical variations.
